title: Microscopic Insights into Strain and Failure Mechanisms in Advanced Semiconductor Packaging
content: In recent years, the semiconductor industry has increasingly focused on advancing packaging technologies, such as 3D heterogeneous integration, to meet the growing demand for smaller, more powerful devices. As transistor node sizes shrink, integrating multiple chiplets into a 3D package has become a pivotal strategy [1]. This requires advanced bonding technologies, such as copper-to-copper (Cu-to-Cu) hybrid bonding, to achieve fine-pitch interconnections (below 10 µm). Cu-to-Cu bonding provides higher-density interconnects than traditional solder bumping by directly interconnecting chiplets [2-4]. In contrast, solder bumping with larger pitch sizes remains essential for many traditional packaging applications, especially where larger interconnects and greater mechanical flexibility are needed [5-7]. The success of these advanced packaging technologies depends heavily on the reliability of the interconnects and the integrity between the formed joints. Strain accumulation at these interfaces, which is caused by cyclic thermo-mechanical stresses during device operation, is a key driver of failure. As these two technologies evolve, understanding their strengths, limitations, and failure mechanisms is critical for ensuring the long-term reliability of semiconductor packages.
